    Part 0: Corpus overview

    The analyzed corpus holds 369 papers, published 2000–2021.

    From seed paper to corpus

    The F1 corpus is built from the bibliography of the seed paper (Lund & Sindbæk 2022): its cited references, treated as a first generation of descendant works. The seed paper’s own reference list resolves to 576 works in the bibliography; the F1 corpus analyzed here holds 369, meaning 207 references were excluded.

    Selection criteria

    Two exclusion criteria were applied when building the F1 set from the seed paper’s reference list:

    • Full books and edited volumes with consolidated bibliographies. A book’s reference list is not comparable in scale or character to a journal article’s, and including it as a single node alongside articles would distort network measures, centrality in particular, that depend on reference-list size.
    • Methodological/technical reports outside the study’s interpretive scope, judged case by case. One paper (Cannell et al. 2016, a geochemical pXRF methods chapter in an edited excavation volume) was excluded on this basis; it remains in the wider bibliography as a citation target for the papers that cite it, but was removed from the annotated F1 seed set.

    No other structured record of exclusion reasons for the remaining works in the seed’s reference list currently exists; this count has not yet been individually itemized and categorized beyond these two documented criteria.

    Corpus composition

    The following sections describe the corpus by publication year, entry type, authorship, venue, and language. Each has a tab for the 369-paper F1 set and a tab for the full bibliography (13,487 live entries).

    Publications by year

    • F1
    • Full corpus

    The corpus spans 2000 to 2021. Publication counts rise over that range rather than sitting flat; 2018 is the single busiest year, with 43 papers.

    The full bibliography spans 1900 to 2023, at true year-by-year resolution; 2008 is the single busiest year, with 493 entries.

    Entry types

    • F1
    • Full corpus

    4 entry types appear in the corpus. The most common, article, accounts for 243 of 369 papers (66%).

    7 entry types appear across the full bibliography. The most common, article, accounts for 5588 of 13486 entries (41%).

    Authorship

    • F1
    • Full corpus

    230 of 369 papers (62%) have a single author. One paper has 17, the largest author count in the corpus.

    This full-corpus count is taken directly from the length of each record’s author list, not from the manually coded author-gender columns used for the F1 tab (those columns were only completed for the 369 F1 papers). 9065 of 13293 entries (68%) have a single listed author. The chart is capped at 10 authors for readability; 75 entries exceed that, including the largest, with 85.

    Publication venues

    • F1
    • Full corpus

    363 of 369 papers are published in an identifiable journal or edited volume (publisher-only records, with neither, are excluded from this chart). The corpus draws on 229 distinct venues across both types, over half of which (192) contribute only a single paper.

    9536 of 13,487 entries are published in an identifiable journal or edited volume; a further 2,163 have only a publisher recorded, typically standalone books, and are excluded from this chart since a publisher is not a comparable unit to a journal or volume title. The full bibliography draws on 5967 distinct journals and volumes, 4850 of which contribute only a single entry.

    Citation detection per F1 paper

    Every F1 paper has at least one resolved outgoing citation, and the citation graph as a whole forms a single connected component. This was not the case throughout corpus construction: extraction passes repeatedly left individual F1 papers disconnected, most often from a reference-list format (footnote-embedded citations, a shared reference section for an edited volume, non-Latin or corrupted encoding) the primary extraction method did not handle, or from the same work being independently extracted twice under two citekeys. Each case was resolved against the original source PDF or documented as a genuine structural exception.

    From detection to resolved bibliography

    The citation graph is built in two stages: automated detection of candidate citations per paper, then manual correction and deduplication across the whole bibliography.

    Raw citation detections by method, before merging duplicate detections of the same citation
    Detection method Raw detections
    Structured reference list (GROBID) 24560
    Inline citation markers 17754
    LLM body-text scan 11487
    Text-pattern matching 10538
    LLM bibliography reparse 1671
    LLM footnote scan 673

    Each paper’s PDF is scanned by six independent methods: GROBID parsing its structured reference list, matching inline citation markers in the body text, text-pattern matching, and three LLM-based passes (a body-text scan, a bibliography reparse, and a footnote scan). A single real citation is frequently flagged by more than one method. The 66,683 raw detections above merge down to 31,994 deduplicated citations per-paper, which are then carried into the bibliography-wide correction process below. The structured reference list and inline-marker matching account for the large majority of raw detections; the LLM-based methods contribute the remainder, recovering citations the structured parser misses, most commonly footnote-embedded references and citations in non-standard or non-Latin formats. 1.16% of bibliography entries (167) have no title recorded: a paper in the corpus cites them, but the entry itself has no title or an incomplete author.

    Once detected, citations are carried into a single shared bibliography, where the same underlying work can be independently detected from multiple citing papers and needs consolidating into one record. This consolidation, along with other manual corrections, is tracked in a running corrections file (corrections.yaml) rather than as edits to the raw pipeline output.

    Manual, individually-reasoned correction actions applied to the bibliography (corrections.yaml)
    Action Count
    set (field corrections: author, year, title, citer lists, etc.) 17528
    delete (fabricated or unresolvable ghost entries removed) 1770
    create (missing entries added from manually verified source data) 960
    merge (duplicate entries combined) 396
    reject (candidate merges/matches checked and confirmed distinct) 80
    split (single entries separated into multiple genuine works) 19

    Two bulk, mechanical field backfills are tracked in the same file but excluded from the table above: a language value was set on 12,807 entries and a detection value on 12,804 entries, both copied wholesale from the pipeline’s own processing cache rather than individually reasoned. Combined they account for more set actions than every other correction in the file put together, so are reported separately to avoid making the file’s manual-correction volume look larger than it is.

    As of this writing the file holds 20753 individually-reasoned correction actions, plus the 25,611 bulk field backfills noted above. The great majority of delete actions removed “ghost” entries: records with no title and no raw citation text, produced when the extraction pipeline generated a placeholder entry it was never able to resolve to a real source. merge actions consolidated cases where the same underlying work had been independently created under two or more citekeys, most commonly because one version came from an automated reference-list extraction with no linked PDF and a second, fuller version was later created when the paper’s own PDF was located and processed directly, or because the same source was independently extracted from two different citing papers’ reference lists, the cross-paper duplication this section exists to resolve. set actions in the table above cover routine field-level corrections: fixing fabricated or garbled author names, correcting mis-parsed years and titles, and adding real citation relationships (cited_by entries) that automated detection missed or failed to resolve on the first pass.

    One deletion in this file was subsequently confirmed incorrect and reversed: a genuine F1 paper had been marked fabricated across multiple earlier review passes despite being a real, verifiable source, and was restored with corrected metadata once checked directly against its source PDF. This is noted here as a reminder that delete corrections, like any other, should be treated as provisional until checked against a primary source rather than as settled fact on the strength of a confident-sounding note.
